Thank you to the Secretary-General for— Thank you to the Secretary-General for convening this workshop and to the Division for Ocean Affairs and the Law of the Sea, DOALOS, for facilitating a New Zealand presentation, as it was not possible to travel from New Zealand for this event. As outlined in New Zealand's report for this workshop, New Zealand takes a very active role in addressing the impacts of bottom fishing on vulnerable marine ecosystems and ensuring the sustainability of deep sea stocks. We do so primarily through the excellent and dedicated work of New Zealand scientists and consistent with the agreed scientific processes and Management Measures of the South Pacific Regional Fisheries Management Organisation, SPRIFMO, and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources, CCAMLR. Both of these organisations manage bottom fishing. They have different legal foundations, different membership, and cover different portions of the world's oceans. But both base their decisions on the best available science. Beginning with SPRIFMO, the New Zealand report sets out in great detail the work undertaken by New Zealand and other SPRIFMO members to develop robust management of bottom fisheries within the convention area. We encourage all workshop participants to read the New Zealand report carefully and to also read the deep well of scientific work on which the report is based. If a SPRIFMO member proposes to undertake bottom fishing within the specified management areas of the convention area, then under the SPRIFMO management framework, they must submit a bottom fishery impact assessment. These bottom fishing impact assessments are assessed by the Scientific Committee. They must be updated at least every 3 years or earlier if there has been a substantial change in the fishery. This ensures that management approaches are based on science and updated as new information becomes available. In 2023, New Zealand, along with Australia, presented a new bottom fishing impact assessment to the SPRIFMO Scientific Committee. This was an update of the earlier 2020 assessment. So this 2023 bottom fishing impact assessment described the management arrangements, the status of the main stocks, the ecological risk assessments, including for interactions with marine mammals, reptiles, seabirds, and the benthic habitats. It also estimated the status of 10 VME indicator taxa within the fishery management areas using the relative benthic status method. The SPRIFMO Scientific Committee accepted this bottom fishing impact assessment, indicating that it represented the best available science, it provided a sound basis for formulating management advice, and it met international standards including the FAO Deep Sea Guidelines. In 2024, New Zealand and Australia updated this bottom fishing impact assessment. This updated assessment applied an alternative dynamic relative benthic status method to incorporate fishery impact data from recent fishing activities. Broadly, This method enabled 3 things. First, the reassessment of taxon-specific depletion and recovery values. Second, the reevaluation of the relationship between estimated habitat suitability and observed abundance. And third, the inclusion of assessments for 7 additional VME indicators. The Scientific Committee then agreed to this revised 2024 Bottom Fishing Impact Assessment incorporating these new methods, and it also agreed that these new methods should be applied to the next update of the Bottom Fishing Impact Assessment, which is scheduled for 2027. And the Scientific Committee agreed to add to its work plan further work to develop and validate abundance models for VME indicator taxa. New Zealand plays an active role in this work. In addition to providing these robust bottom fishing impact assessments, in 2025, New Zealand led the review of the bottom fishing impact assessment standard for SPRIFMO. So in reviewing the standards for these bottom fishing impact assessments, New Zealand considered the overarching objectives for bottom fishing impact assessments and how these relate to relevant conservation and management measures. as well as other relevant instruments such as the stock assessment framework. As a result, the improved bottom fishing impact standard will be used to inform the next bottom fishing impact assessment. As I noted earlier, this is scheduled to be considered by the SPRIFMO Scientific Committee in 2027. Of course, in addition to assessing the impacts of bottom fishing, it is essential to also regularly assess the status of the stocks. Since 2022, New Zealand has presented 2 deep-sea stock assessments to SPRIFMO. This includes the orange roughy stocks for Louis Ridge, West Norfolk Ridge, Lord Howe Rise, and the northwest Challenger Plateau in 2022, and an assessment of orange ruffy stocks in the Challenger Plateau in 2024. A further stock assessment for the Challenger Plateau is due in 2028. New Zealand is also conducting a specialist technical review the orange roughy stock structure on the Westpac Bank and the adjacent New Zealand EEZ in the Tasman Sea. The objectives of this work are to review aspects of orange roughy science, including data collection, biological parameters, and assessment approaches. This will then inform the ongoing science work plan for New Zealand's orange roughy fisheries, both domestically and in the SPRIFMO Convention area. In addition to this work on target species, management of bycatch and impacts on non-target species is an essential component of fisheries management. This is reflected in the SPRIFMO Conservation and Management Measure, for the management of bottom fishing. Under this measure, the Scientific Committee is required to provide advice to the Commission on the extent of interactions between bottom fishing and species of concern and to provide any recommendations for management action as a consequence. New Zealand again with Australia has led analysis on the impacts of bottom fishing on species of concern. This includes the presentation of papers to the Scientific Committee in 2022 and 2024. As a result of this work, the Scientific Committee noted that the capture of marine mammals, seabirds, and reptiles are rare in the spritmo bottom fisheries. The Scientific Committee agreed that there was no need at this time for additional measures, but as I already noted, it is a requirement for the Scientific Committee to regularly review the impact of bottom fishing on species of concern. And further to this, New Zealand-led work over the last 2 years to promote the adoption of a strengthened measure for minimising bycatch of seabirds in the SPRIFMO Convention area. The Commission adopted this measure at its meeting in February 2026. Fisheries managers— it's also critical that there are robust places processes in place in the event that there is an incident which may cause significant adverse impact from bottom fishing on vulnerable marine ecosystems. This regime is set out in the SPRIFMO Conservation and Management Measure, which regulates bottom fishing. This measure sets out the obligations for members if their vessels have bycatch of VME indicator taxa at or above prescribed thresholds. These thresholds are based on a precautionary approach and are within the lower end of parameters established by the Scientific Committee in 2021. In 2025, the Scientific Committee reaffirmed that these parameters are still based on the best available science available for setting the encounter threshold. So in addition to the move-on obligation for the vessel concerned, there is also a requirement for the flag state to undertake a thorough review of the encounter. The flag state must provide a report to the Scientific Committee which indicates whether a VME was present in the encounter area and whether the encounter was likely to have caused significant adverse impacts. This report from the flag state should also include any management recommendations as a result of the encounter. These recommendations are then considered by the Scientific Committee with final decisions made by the Commission. To aid in this process, SPRIFMO has adopted an encounter review standard. New Zealand led the development of this standard and SPRIFMO adopted it in 2024. This was the first time that a regional fisheries management organisation Managing Deep Sea Fisheries had adopted such a standard. This encounter review standard provides clear guidelines for carrying out reviews of encounters with potential VMEs. It sets out the process for the Scientific Committee when it considers the reviews of encounters and delivers advice to the Commission. Under this process, New Zealand is currently updating our review of a particular encounter by a New Zealand vessel in the Tasman Sea in 2024. This update will take into account additional information which was not available at the time of New Zealand's original review of this encounter. We expect to submit this updated encounter review to the Scientific Committee in September. New Zealand is actively involved in the SPRIFMO management framework for bottom fishing to ensure that it is underpinned by the best available science. I have set out our involvement in the regular updates to the bottom fishing conservation and management measure, the bottom fishing impact assessments, and the encounter standards. Looking ahead, New Zealand continues to invest in science to support the sustainable management of RIFMO fisheries. Currently, New Zealand is exploring alternative approaches using ecological bioregions as the basis for spatial management. We hope that this might provide the means to prevent significant adverse impacts on VMEs whilst maintaining appropriate fishing opportunities. Turning now to the Antarctic and the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources, CCAMLR. New Zealand is a founding and active member of this commission established in 1986. CCAMLR has a well-developed management framework for its bottom fisheries. This level of cautionary management aligns with its status. CCAMLR is not a regional fisheries management organisation. It is part of the Antarctic Treaty System. And has a single objective: conservation. All of the measures relevant to CCAMLR's comprehensive management of bottom fishing were in place in 2022 when New Zealand last reported into this particular process. Within CCAMLR, the focus is on implementation of these measures. Since 2022, Additional VME and VME risk areas have been identified under the relevant CCAMLR conservation measures, and these areas have been closed to, to bottom fishing. The processes and evidence used for the identification, reporting, and management of VMEs are the subject of continuous improvement work. New Zealand has continued to undertake scientific research to identify where VMEs are likely to occur, and to verify areas classified as either potential or designated VMEs in the Ross Sea region. New Zealand vessels participating in the Ross Sea exploratory fishery collect data. This is collected by observers on those vessels and also by the fishers themselves. Data is also collected by New Zealand scientific research vessels the Ross Sea. And all of this feeds into New Zealand's scientific contribution to CCAMLR. New Zealand also undertakes the Ross Sea Shelf Survey of toothfish and the stock assessment for the Ross Sea Exploratory Toothfish Fishery. This world-leading stock assessment underpins CCAMLR's precautionary management of I've outlined a number of method— measures from both SPRIFMO and CAMLA for the effective management of the impacts of bottom fishing. But it is also critical that there are effective monitoring, control, and surveillance mechanisms in place. Across both SPRIFMO and CAMLA, in line with relevant obligations, New Zealand deploys observers on our flagged vessels. In addition, New Zealand conducts aerial and surface patrolling in the Pacific and Southern Oceans to monitor compliance and deter and detect IUU This is a vital contribution to ensuring that we can achieve the goals of sustainably managed fishing, bottom fishing. While it was not possible for experts from New Zealand to attend this workshop in person, we look forward to a report on the discussions. And I encourage any interested participants to read New Zealand's report in full and to reach out to New Zealand officials if you have any questions. Thank you and best wishes for the remainder of the workshop. Ngā mihi.

Muchas gracias. Allow me to share employment, knowledge, and life for the coastal communities. Spain's experience is not unique, but I offer this as a way of understanding our experience on the basis of the best available scientific evidence. Evidence. We're open to innovation, and this has been built on the basis of cooperation across administrations, science, and the fishing sector, which is providing experience and knowledge and insight. And so the first question we had to ask ourselves is, what is it that we are trying to preserve and protect? When we talk about vulnerable marine ecosystems, we're talking about some of the highest ecological value in the ocean. These are habitats that house enormous amounts of biodiversity. They fulfill essential roles and they also contribute to the resilience of marine ecosystems and they represent natural heritage that is of extraordinary value. And so preserving this cannot be up for debate. Preserving these vulnerable marine ecosystems is part of and it should be a part of a responsibility that we must all share. But oceans, and we should never forget, do not just represent ecological value. They also— the oceans sustain human activity, and this is fundamental for maintaining our societies. The ocean provides healthy foods, employment, economic activity, food security, and it keeps a number of coastal communities alive. It also preserves knowledge, tradition, and cultural heritage that has been passed down from generation to generation. So when we talk about defending the fishing sector, we shouldn't be referring only to an economic activity of fishing, but rather defending a whole set of values that fishing brings to society. And so the question is not just about how can we hold on to value but really how to manage it all as a whole. And from our perspective, this is the real challenge. Preservation and fishing often are presented as in contrast or in opposition to one another, and this is rather simplistic. In the regional fisheries management organizations, we have seen that there is compatibility here. Vulnerable marine ecosystems are ecological goods that we should preserve, and the fishing sector also represents a good for society, and this should also be maintained. Both of these are part of the general interest, and so the modern management that we should apply should therefore not just be limited to protecting one or the other. This system, this management does not mean giving up on protecting VMEs. Rather, we should seek strategies that allow us to reconcile both of these values using knowledge, innovation, and dialogue. And so how can we bring this about? How can we improve this management? So starting from knowledge, science is the foundation for any responsible decision. And in addition to knowing about the existence of vulnerable marine ecosystems, it's also important to know how the different types of fishing gear interact with these different marine ecosystems. We need to be aware of the real risks that each of these activities has on the environment. We need to know about the frequency of interaction, the intensity of interaction. intensity of these interactions taking place and the spatial scale that we're talking about. And ultimately, when decisions are taken, we need to know about all of the consequences of the decision or activity. And we also need continuous follow-up because decisions should not be static. They should not be one-offs. They need to evolve in accordance with new technological solutions and as new information emerges. And here I want to highlight the importance of innovation. This is not just an accessory point. This is crucial, and this is going to allow us to continuously improve and explore solutions before resorting to restrictive measures. And so how do we take the best possible decisions? As I said earlier, we are basing our decisions on information and knowledge. Science helps us assess the impacts, the risks, and assess the efficiency, but science doesn't actually take the decisions. This responsibility falls on us, the administrators, the managers. It is our role on the basis of the available scientific information and taking into account all public interests, it is down to us to apply all of the measures that allow us to maintain and preserve vulnerable marine ecosystems and also ensure the sustainability of the fishing sector by ensuring food security, employment, social cohesion, and also cultural heritage. And so we should talk also about taking effective decisions that are proportionate and well-suited. The decisions also need to be continuously reviewed and adjusted in light of new results. And so from improvements in knowledge and progress in technology. And I want to just say a few words about how the different types of fishing gear interact. Do they all interact in the same way with VMEs? I think the answer is no. Each type of fishing gear has a different type of interaction. It depends on a number of factors. factor. Is it active or is it a passive type of fishing? What type of species? Are they benthic? Are they pelagic? And so on. What type of contact do they have with the ocean floor? There are many different ways for this interaction to occur. And so for all of these reasons, I think it's important that we should avoid these general or generalized approaches and we should use specific knowledge about each type of fishing on how they operate and what frequency and what their real impact is on VMEs and the ones that they can have an impact on. And so knowing about these differences and these distinctions will allow us to design adapted management measures that are better suited and better proportioned. And what about innovation? And so the profiles can be— the interaction profiles can be adapted. And here innovation plays a fundamental role. As I was saying, I would like to present 2 examples of technical modifications based on innovation that have had significant impacts in terms of reducing the impact on VMEs. And one of these is stone ball longline. And this, thanks to some adjustments to its configuration, has totally changed the profile of interaction with the seabed. It reduces interaction with the seabed and it uses a system of weights and floats that allows the gear to maintain its function without, or at least in a very limited way, way impacting the seabed and the VMEs. It is extremely selective, this stone ball longline gear. Another example of technological innovation are the flying doors. This is another example of an innovation that has considerably altered the pattern of interaction of the gear with the seabed. Again, as I said, we reduce the contact with the seabed and of the trawl itself, and this overall reduces quite significantly the impact on the VME. It reduces the friction, and you also get also a significant reduction in fuel consumption and also in the carbon footprint of the emissions. These are just 2 examples. I'm not suggesting these as universal solutions. These are just adaptations that facilitate this reconciliation of marine ecosystems and fishing. And so what have we learned? On the basis of these experiences, we can extract a few conclusions. The first of these, and I think we heard a little bit about this earlier or yesterday from the RFMOs, it is possible to ensure compatibility. This is not automatic. It is the outcome of good governance and good cooperation, joint management. This requires deep scientific knowledge, support, cooperation, and innovation to seek solutions, and it also requires a lot of participation from the fishing sector to provide practical experience and feedback. And so I will wrap up this presentation highlighting the key— 3 key takeaway messages that I want to leave you with. Firstly, science must guide our decisions. Without science, we cannot know about the ecosystems, we cannot evaluate the risks, and we cannot measure the effectiveness of the measures that we're implementing. Innovation also has the capacity to improve management. It helps us seek more effective, more efficient, and more proportionate solutions that are better adapted and better suited to reality. And finally, adaptive management should allow us to maintain sustainable VMEs and also a sustainable fishing sector. And so our goal is not to choose, but rather to manage both of these goals. And Spain's commitment is to continue working in this direction with science, innovation, and cooperation, seeking adaptive fisheries for future generations. I thank you.

As global concerns over ocean health grow, bottom trawling has become the focus of scrutiny in numerous fora encompassing environmental, climate-related, socioeconomic, and food security concerns. Given Brazil's current COP30 presidency and the integration of aquatic food systems into the global climate agenda, I would focus my presentation on the debate on the potential and actual climate impact of pot trolling. The growing interest in deep-sea resources exploitation beyond fisheries has shed light on our limited knowledge regarding the impact of deep-sea anthropogenic disturbances and the potential cumulative threats to seabed species and ecosystems. Pot trawling is a primary driver of physical disturbance on the seabed, but the extent of its direct and indirect climate impacts remains unclear. Some scientific studies have identified bottom trawling as a significant source of atmospheric carbon emissions. These studies are based on the finding that fishing gears displaces not only target species but also organic and inorganic matter accumulated on the seafloor over potentially thousands of years. In doing so, bottom trawling triggers biological and chemical processes that convert carbon previously deposited in the seabed into carbon dioxide. This process may be releasing significant amounts of CO2 into the atmosphere while diminishing the seafloor's capacity to serve as a long-term carbon sink. One study estimates that up to 60% of the released CO2 reaches the atmosphere within 9 years of the trawling event. This process could also contribute to acidification of trolled zones, and alterations in benthic trophic cycles could affect phytoplankton, negatively influencing the ocean's overall efficiency in sequestering carbon through photosynthesis. Recent studies have contested this assumption that bottom trawling is a significant source of carbon emission. When comparing trolled areas with untrawled areas, it has been observed that in at least 60% of cases there was no significant difference in the amount of carbon stored. They also contend that extrapolating findings from localized studies to global scale leads to high levels of scientific uncertainty, which policymakers should consider with caution. Another climate-related concern regarding bottom trawling is the intensive use of fossil fuel. In fact, fossil combustion for vessel propulsion is the primary source of greenhouse gas emission in wild capture fisheries. The global fishing fleets consist of more than 4.5 million vessels, which produce an estimated 0.5% of total global GHG emissions. In this realm, bottom trawling stands out for its high fuel intensity, and fuel is consumed mainly during fishing operations rather than during transit, as it's observed in other fishing methods. The energy intensity performance of trawlers varies considerably, but studies indicate that capture of flatfish species by bottle trawling can require up to 7 times more fuel than fishing with gillnets or purse seines, and others indicate that the average fuel use intensity— it means liters of fuel per ton of fish captured— for crustacean trawling is 2 to 3 times higher than for purse seining. To integrate the debate on bottom trawling footprint into the broader debate on fisheries mitigation and adaptation and aquatic food systems transformation as a whole. In this debate, the central role bottom trawling plays in global aquatic food production cannot be disregarded. It accounts for 25% of wild-caught seafood providing livelihoods for hundreds of thousands of workers and their families and securing food and nutrition for millions, for us included.
